analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums based on genetic information.
analysis.headline: A bill with 213 House cosponsors — more than 40% of the House, both Democrats and Republicans — never got a vote in any committee and died when the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for health insurers, employer health plans, and Medicare supplement (Medigap) issuers to deny, cancel, refuse to renew, or reprice coverage because of a person's genetic information or because they sought genetic testing. It also would have barred insurers from demanding genetic information and required written consent before sharing it, with compensatory and punitive damages for violations. It sat in three House committees and subcommittees for the entire two-year Congress and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with a family history of genetic disease, people considering genetic testing, and their relatives. The bill covered genetic information about family members, so a relative's diagnosis could not be used against you. It would also have made people safer getting genetic tests, since the results could not follow them to an insurer.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and insurers from denying, canceling, refusing to renew, or varying premiums and terms of coverage based on genetic information or on having requested or received genetic services.
Extends the same protections to the individual insurance market and to Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies.
Bars plans and insurers from requesting or requiring genetic information from participants, and blocks disclosure of genetic information without prior written authorization for each disclosure.
Gives people harmed by violations the right to sue for compensatory, consequential, and punitive damages.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employer plans, and Medigap issuers lose a pricing tool: they could no longer use genetic information to screen out or surcharge people likely to need care. Some of that cost could spread across premium payers if higher-risk applicants enroll who previously would have been denied.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips insurers of genetic underwriting entirely. If people who learn they carry a disease risk buy full coverage while people without that risk buy less, insurers bear unpredictable costs that could push premiums up for everyone in the pool — the standard objection to any rule forbidding risk-based pricing. The bill contains no provision addressing that cost, such as reinsurance or risk adjustment.

The bill covers health insurance only. It does nothing about discrimination by employers, life insurers, or disability insurers, so genetic information could still be used against a person in hiring or in buying life insurance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is genuinely valuable — it targets a real, foreseeable harm as genetic testing spread, and it includes real enforcement teeth. The honest cost is that forbidding genetic pricing entirely, with no mechanism to spread the added risk, could modestly raise premiums across the pool. The coverage gap for employment and life insurance is a real limitation, though fixing it would have made the bill harder to pass. On balance the protection for people with genetic risk outweighs the spread cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees in January 1997, none of them ever brought it up, a petition to force it out of committee never got the signatures it needed, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 7, 1997, and referred to the Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees.
Within weeks it was sent to three subcommittees — Health, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations — where no action followed for the rest of the Congress.

With 213 cosponsors and no committee movement, sponsor Louise Slaughter filed a motion to discharge the committees in June 1998 — a procedure that would force the bill to the floor if a majority of House members signed the petition. Petition 105-4 never gathered enough signatures and no vote ever occurred.
The 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and Medigap issuers came out ahead: they kept the freedom to use genetic information in deciding who gets covered and at what price, and faced no damages liability. No protection for patients was enacted in this Congress; a federal genetic nondiscrimination law covering health insurance and employment did not pass until 2008 (GINA), eleven years later.

for.name: Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 43 original cosponsors and, after the bill sat untouched for 16 months, filed a discharge petition to try to force it to the House floor.

for.name: House cosponsors of H.R. 306
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from nearly half the House — far more than needed to pass if it had reached a vote.

against.name: House Commerce Committee (Chair Tom Bliley)
against.role: Primary committee of referral, R chair
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on day one and referred it to its Health and Environment Subcommittee; neither committee nor subcommittee held a markup or reported the bill in two years.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of referral (jurisdiction over employer plans and the tax code provisions)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on January 21, 1997; no action followed for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of referral (jurisdiction over employer-employee benefits)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on January 31, 1997; no action followed.

against.name: House members who declined to sign the discharge petition
against.role: Majority of the House needed to sign to force a floor vote
against.what_they_did: Petition 105-4, filed June 11, 1998, never attracted the signatures of a House majority, so the bill stayed locked in committee despite its 213 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 185 Democrats, 27 Republicans, and 1 Independent of 213 — but the three committees that buried the bill were all chaired by Republicans, and no committee ever reported it.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from using genetic information to deny, cancel, or reprice coverage, and from demanding or sharing genetic data without consent. Insurers' underwriting advantage over people with genetic risk runs directly against those people's access to coverage.
Medigap policy issuers would have lost the ability to deny or condition policies or vary pricing based on genetic information, and would face damages suits for violations.

By making test results unusable against a patient's insurance, the bill would have made people far more willing to undergo genetic testing and counseling, expanding demand for genetic services. Providers and patients stood on the same side.
